title: Food tests
aim: To use qualitative reagents to test a range of foods for the presence of reducing sugars, starch, protein and lipids.
background: Food contains carbohydrates, proteins and lipids. Carbohydrates include sugars, such as glucose, and starch, which is a large molecule made of many glucose units joined together. Proteins are made of long chains of amino acids. Lipids (fats and oils) are made of glycerol and fatty acids. Each type of molecule can be detected with a chemical reagent that changes colour when the molecule is present.

Benedict's test detects reducing sugars such as glucose (sucrose is not a reducing sugar). The food sample is heated with blue Benedict's solution in a water bath; a positive result is a change to green, yellow, orange or brick red, depending on how much sugar is present. Iodine solution detects starch, turning from orange-brown to blue-black. Biuret reagent detects protein, turning from blue to purple (lilac).

Lipids can be detected with Sudan III stain, which dissolves in lipids and gives a red-stained oily layer on top of the liquid. Another test is the ethanol emulsion test: the food is shaken with ethanol, then the ethanol is poured into water, and a cloudy white emulsion forms if lipid is present. These tests are qualitative: they show whether a substance is present, and Benedict's test can give a rough indication of how much sugar there is.
hypothesis: Glucose solution will give a positive Benedict's test, potato will give a positive iodine test for starch, egg white will give a positive biuret test for protein, and vegetable oil will give a positive Sudan III test for lipid. Distilled water will give negative results for every test.

variables.independent: Type of food tested (glucose solution, potato, egg white, vegetable oil, milk, and distilled water as a control).
variables.dependent: Colour change (or appearance) with each reagent, showing whether reducing sugar, starch, protein or lipid is present.
control: Same volume of food solution in each test (2 cm³)
Same volume of each reagent added
Same water bath temperature (about 75 °C) and heating time (5 minutes) for Benedict's test
Clean test tubes and pipettes used for each sample to prevent cross-contamination

equipment: Food samples (for example glucose solution, potato, egg white, vegetable oil, milk)
Test tubes and test tube rack
Biuret reagent (or sodium hydroxide solution and copper sulfate solution)
Water bath set to about 75 °C (or a beaker of hot water from a kettle)
method: Prepare each solid food: grind a small piece with distilled water using a pestle and mortar to make a paste, then add more distilled water and stir.
Filter the mixture through filter paper in a funnel to get a clear solution, or leave it to settle. Liquid foods can be used directly or diluted.
Benedict's test for reducing sugars: put 2 cm³ of food solution in a test tube and add 2 cm³ (an equal volume) of Benedict's solution.
Place the test tube in a water bath at about 75 °C for 5 minutes. Record the final colour: blue (negative), or green, yellow, orange or brick red (positive, increasing amounts of sugar).

Iodine test for starch: put a few drops of food solution (or a small piece of solid food) into a dimple of a spotting tile and add 2 drops of iodine solution. Record the colour: orange-brown (negative) or blue-black (positive).

Biuret test for protein: put 2 cm³ of food solution in a test tube and add 2 cm³ of biuret reagent. Shake gently and leave for a few minutes. Record the colour: blue (negative) or purple/lilac (positive).

Sudan III test for lipids: put 2 cm³ of food solution in a test tube and add 3 drops of Sudan III stain. Shake gently and allow to settle. A red-stained oily layer on the surface shows that lipid is present.

Alternative lipid test (ethanol emulsion test): shake a small amount of food with 2 cm³ of ethanol, then pour the ethanol into a test tube containing 2 cm³ of distilled water. A cloudy white emulsion shows that lipid is present.
Carry out every test on distilled water as a negative control, so you can compare colours.
Use a clean pipette and test tube for each sample, and record all results in a table.

safety.risk: Scalds from hot water or a hot test tube.
safety.precaution: Use a test tube holder, point the open end of the tube away from people, and do not heat Benedict's solution directly in a flame.

safety.risk: Irritant or corrosive to eyes and skin.
safety.precaution: Wear eye protection, use small volumes and wash any splashes off skin immediately with plenty of water.

safety.risk: Highly flammable; vapour could catch fire.
safety.precaution: Keep ethanol away from all naked flames: use an electric water bath, not a Bunsen burner, when ethanol is in use.

safety.hazard: Iodine solution, Sudan III and Benedict's solution
safety.risk: Irritate eyes and stain skin; Sudan III is dissolved in a flammable solvent.
safety.precaution: Wear eye protection, use dropping bottles to add small amounts, and keep Sudan III away from flames.

safety.risk: Food in the laboratory may be contaminated with chemicals; allergens such as egg or milk.
safety.precaution: Never eat food used in the laboratory, and check for allergies before handling samples.

rows: Reducing sugar, protein and lipid present
results.notes: Record the colour after each test, not just 'positive' or 'negative'. Compare each colour with the distilled water control. With Benedict's, the colour gives a rough idea of how much reducing sugar is present: green (a trace), yellow, orange, brick red (a lot). Milk contains lactose, a reducing sugar, so it turns orange.

analysis: Glucose solution gave a brick-red colour with Benedict's solution, showing a high concentration of reducing sugar. Milk turned orange, showing a moderate amount of reducing sugar (lactose).
Potato turned iodine blue-black, showing that it contains starch. This is because potato tubers store carbohydrate as starch.
Egg white and milk turned biuret reagent purple, showing that they contain protein.
Vegetable oil and milk formed a red-stained layer with Sudan III, showing that they contain lipid.
Distilled water was negative in every test. This control shows the colour of each reagent with no nutrient present and confirms that any colour change was caused by substances in the food.

The tests are qualitative, so they only show whether a nutrient is present. To compare amounts, a colorimeter or a set of colour standards made with known glucose concentrations could be used for the Benedict's test.

errors.error: Judging colours by eye is subjective, especially the in-between Benedict's colours such as green or yellow.
errors.improvement: Compare with a set of colour standards of known concentration, view against a white background, or use a colorimeter to measure the colour.

errors.error: Cross-contamination from reusing pipettes or test tubes could give false positive results.
errors.improvement: Use a clean pipette and test tube for each food and each reagent, and rinse the pestle and mortar between foods.

errors.error: Different volumes of food solution or reagent, or different heating times, make the intensity of colours hard to compare.
errors.improvement: Measure volumes with a measuring cylinder or graduated pipette, and heat every Benedict's tube for the same time at the same temperature.

errors.error: A cloudy food solution can hide colour changes.
errors.improvement: Filter the ground food solution to give a clear liquid before testing.

examTips: Learn each test as three parts: the reagent, what it tests for, and the colour change from negative to positive. For example: biuret, protein, blue to purple.
Benedict's test must be heated (in a water bath at about 75 °C). The other tests are carried out without heating.
Say 'blue-black' for a positive starch test, not just 'black' or 'blue'. Iodine starts orange-brown.
Benedict's test is semi-quantitative: green, yellow, orange then brick red show increasing amounts of reducing sugar.
Never heat ethanol with a Bunsen burner: it is highly flammable.

questions.question: Which reagent is used to test for starch?
markScheme: 1 mark: iodine solution
questions.explanation: Iodine solution turns from orange-brown to blue-black when starch is present. Benedict's tests for reducing sugars, biuret for protein and Sudan III for lipids.

questions.question: What is the colour of a positive result for protein with biuret reagent?
markScheme: 1 mark: purple (lilac or mauve)
questions.explanation: Biuret reagent is blue and turns purple when protein is present. Brick red is a positive Benedict's result, blue-black is positive for starch and orange-brown is the colour of iodine solution itself.

questions.question: Describe how to test a food solution for reducing sugar, and give the colour of a positive result.
markScheme: 1 mark: add (an equal volume of) Benedict's solution
1 mark: heat in a (hot) water bath (about 75 °C) for a few minutes
1 mark: positive colour: green, yellow, orange or brick red (from blue)
questions.explanation: Benedict's test is the only food test that needs heating. The final colour depends on the amount of reducing sugar, from green for a trace to brick red for a large amount.

questions.question: A food sample gives a blue-black colour with iodine and stays blue after heating with Benedict's solution. What does the food contain?
markScheme: 1 mark: starch but no reducing sugar
questions.explanation: Blue-black with iodine means starch is present. Benedict's staying blue is a negative result, so there is no reducing sugar. Starch is made of glucose units but is not itself a reducing sugar, so it does not react with Benedict's solution.

questions.question: Describe how the ethanol emulsion test is used to show that a food contains lipid.
markScheme: 1 mark: shake the food with ethanol, then pour (the ethanol) into water
1 mark: a cloudy white emulsion forms if lipid is present
questions.explanation: Lipids dissolve in ethanol but not in water. When the ethanol is added to water, the lipid comes out of solution as tiny droplets, which make the liquid look cloudy white.

questions.question: Four food samples were heated with Benedict's solution. Which final colour shows the highest concentration of reducing sugar?
markScheme: 1 mark: brick red
questions.explanation: The colour sequence with increasing reducing sugar is blue (none), green, yellow, orange, brick red. Brick red shows the most sugar.

questions.question: Explain why distilled water is also tested with each reagent.
acceptedAnswers: shows colour change is due to the food
markScheme: 1 mark: it acts as a (negative) control
1 mark: to show the colour of a negative result / to compare, so any colour change must be caused by the food
questions.explanation: The control shows what each reagent looks like when the nutrient is absent. This makes it easier to spot small colour changes and shows the reagents themselves are not contaminated.

questions.question: Give one hazard in the food tests practical and describe how to reduce the risk.
acceptedAnswers: hot water bath scald use test tube holder
markScheme: 1 mark: hazard, for example hot water bath, flammable ethanol, irritant biuret reagent or iodine
1 mark: matching precaution, for example use a test tube holder, keep ethanol away from flames, wear eye protection
questions.explanation: A good answer pairs a specific hazard with a specific precaution. 'Be careful' is not enough: say exactly what you would do.

questions.question: Why is solid food ground with distilled water and filtered before testing?
options: To break down starch into sugars
To make a solution of the food so the reagents can mix with it and colours are easy to see
To kill any bacteria in the food
To remove the lipids from the food
markScheme: 1 mark: to release nutrients into solution so reagents can react, and filtering removes solid bits that hide the colour
questions.explanation: Grinding breaks open cells so nutrients dissolve in the water. Filtering gives a clear liquid, so colour changes are not hidden by cloudiness. Grinding does not digest starch; that needs the enzyme amylase.

questions.question:
A student wants to make 10 cm³ of 0.5% glucose solution to use as a colour standard. They have a 2% glucose solution and distilled water.
Calculate the volume of 2% glucose solution needed.
markScheme: 1 mark: 0.5 ÷ 2 = 0.25 (dilution factor)
1 mark: 0.25 × 10 = 2.5 cm³ (made up to 10 cm³ with 7.5 cm³ distilled water)
questions.explanation: The new solution must be one quarter as concentrated, so one quarter of the final volume is the stock solution: 10 × 0.5 ÷ 2 = 2.5 cm³ of 2% glucose plus 7.5 cm³ of water.

questions.question: Food tests are described as qualitative. Suggest how the Benedict's test could be adapted to compare the concentration of reducing sugar in two fruit juices more objectively.
markScheme: 1 mark: make a set of colour standards using known concentrations of glucose (and compare), or use a colorimeter
1 mark: use the same volumes of juice and Benedict's and the same heating time and temperature
questions.explanation: Judging colour by eye is subjective. Comparing with standards of known concentration, or measuring the colour with a colorimeter, gives a more objective, semi-quantitative result.

questions.question: Which result shows that a food contains lipid when tested with Sudan III stain?
options: The solution turns brick red after heating
A red-stained oily layer forms on top of the liquid
markScheme: 1 mark: a red-stained (oily) layer separates out on the surface
questions.explanation: Sudan III dissolves in lipids and stains them red. Lipids are less dense than water and do not mix with it, so they form a red layer on top.

questions.question: Milk turned orange with Benedict's solution, purple with biuret reagent and formed a red layer with Sudan III. State which nutrients milk contains.
markScheme: 1 mark: reducing sugar and protein
1 mark: lipid (fat)
questions.explanation: Each positive result points to one nutrient: orange with Benedict's shows reducing sugar (lactose), purple with biuret shows protein, and the red layer with Sudan III shows lipid.

questions.question:
A student is given an unknown food. Describe how the student could find out whether the food contains starch, protein and lipid.
Include the reagents used and the positive results.
markScheme: Indicative content: grind food with distilled water using pestle and mortar, filter; starch: add iodine solution (few drops on spotting tile), positive blue-black from orange-brown; protein: add equal volume of biuret reagent to food solution, positive purple from blue; lipid: add Sudan III, positive red oily layer on top, or shake food with ethanol then pour into water, positive cloudy white emulsion; use distilled water control; clean equipment between tests; eye protection; no flames with ethanol
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): clear, logically ordered descriptions of all three tests with correct reagents and positive colours, plus food preparation or a control.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): describes two tests correctly, or all three with some errors or missing colours.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): names one or two reagents or colours with little method.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Notice the question does not ask about sugars, so Benedict's test earns no marks here. Top answers give the reagent, the method and the starting and final colours for each test.

questions.question:
A student wants to find out which of three fruit juices contains the most reducing sugar.
Describe how the student could use the Benedict's test to compare the juices and make the results valid.
markScheme: Indicative content: add the same volume of each juice (for example 2 cm³) to separate test tubes; add the same volume of Benedict's solution to each; heat in the same water bath at the same temperature (about 75 °C) for the same time; compare final colours (green, yellow, orange, brick red) against a white background; the colour nearest brick red shows the most reducing sugar; include a distilled water control; use colour standards made from known glucose concentrations or a colorimeter to make the comparison objective; repeat each test
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear method with at least two control variables and a valid way of comparing the colours to decide which juice has most reducing sugar.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): states that Benedict's solution is added and heated and the colours compared, with little control of variables.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: To compare amounts, everything except the juice must stay the same: volumes, temperature and heating time. Because Benedict's test is only semi-quantitative, colour standards or a colorimeter make the comparison more objective.
